name: Pyramid
function: Ventral surface bundle of the medulla formed by corticospinal fibers descending from the basis pontis, flanking the anterior median fissure; at the cervicomedullary junction roughly 85-90 percent of its axons cross in the pyramidal decussation to become the lateral corticospinal tract, the remainder continuing as the anterior corticospinal tract.

afferent: Corticospinal fibers of the basis pontis (tract-corticospinal-lateral)
efferent: Pyramidal decussation (tract-pyramidal-decussation) to the contralateral lateral corticospinal tract

clinical.findings: Unilateral pyramidal infarction (medial medullary syndrome) weakens the opposite body below the face; because decussation lies caudal to the medulla, deficits are contralateral and the face is typically spared.

clinical.syndrome: Crossed hemiparesis — the brainstem signature of a pre-decussation lesion
clinical.findings: Above the decussation every corticospinal lesion is crossed relative to the accompanying cranial-nerve deficit, which is what generates the brainstem syndrome families: ipsilateral CN III palsy with contralateral hemiparesis (Weber), ipsilateral CN VI and VII palsies with contralateral hemiparesis (Millard-Gubler), and ipsilateral tongue weakness with contralateral hemiparesis (Déjerine). The pyramid is the last station at which the bundle is still uncrossed, and therefore the level at which the pattern reverses.
clinical.vascular: Anterior spinal artery / basilar paramedian perforators
clinical.note: The face is spared by a pyramid lesion because corticobulbar fibres cross separately — a useful discriminator from a capsular stroke, in which face and limbs weaken together.

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed., Ch. "Corticospinal Tract and Other Motor Pathways"
Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed., Ch. "Brainstem II: Internal Structures and Vascular Supply"

name: Pyramidal decussation
function: The great motor crossover at the cervicomedullary junction: the majority of corticospinal axons sweep posteromedially across the midline, interrupting the anterior median fissure, so that each cerebral hemisphere commands the opposite half of the body. The crossing fibers remodel the internal architecture of the closed medulla, displacing the gray matter laterally.

efferent: Contralateral lateral corticospinal tract of the spinal cord (tract-corticospinal-lateral)

bloodSupply: Anterior spinal artery and vertebral branches

clinical.findings: Lesions at the decussation (Chiari malformation, foramen magnum tumors) produce a characteristic cruciate paralysis: arm-predominant weakness from damage to the crossing fibers of the hand area, which decussate most caudally.
clinical.note: Leg fibers cross more rostrally, sparing the lower limbs in partial lesions.

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed., Ch. "Corticospinal Tract and Other Motor Pathways"
Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed., Ch. "Brainstem I: Surface Anatomy and Cross-Sectional Anatomy"

name: Internal arcuate fibers
function: The sensory decussation: second-order axons of the gracile and cuneate nuclei sweep ventromedially around the central gray, cross the midline as a broad sheet ventral to the central canal, and pivot rostrally to form the contralateral medial lemniscus — the handoff at which each medial lemniscus comes to represent the opposite half of the body.

efferent: Contralateral medial lemniscus (tract-medial-lemniscus) ascending to VPL

bloodSupply: Anterior spinal artery and vertebral perforators

clinical.syndrome: Side-of-deficit flip at the sensory decussation
clinical.findings: Because the internal arcuate fibers cross here, the laterality of a dorsal-column lesion flips at exactly this point: injury of the fasciculus or of the gracile/cuneate nucleus at or below the decussation (foramen magnum tumor, Chiari malformation, high cervical fracture-dislocation) removes vibration, joint-position sense and discriminative touch on the SAME side as the lesion, whereas damage to the medial lemniscus just above it produces the contralateral loss of the medial medullary syndrome. Midline involvement of the crossing sheet gives bilateral loss with sensory ataxia, pseudoathetosis and a positive Romberg sign.
clinical.vascular: Anterior spinal artery and vertebral perforators
clinical.note: The most examinable fact about this structure: the side of the sensory deficit tells you whether the lesion sits in the dorsal columns, in the decussation itself, or in the medial lemniscus above it.

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed., Ch. "Somatosensory Pathways"
Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed., Ch. "Brainstem II: Internal Structures and Vascular Supply"

name: Fasciculus gracilis
function: Medial dorsal-column bundle conveying, uncrossed and somatotopically ordered, large-fiber touch, vibration, two-point discrimination and conscious proprioception from the lower limb and lower trunk (below about T6) up to the nucleus gracilis; medial in the dorsal funiculus at every cord and lower-medullary level.

afferent: Dorsal root (large-fiber) afferents of the lower trunk and lower limb ascending ipsilaterally
efferent: Nucleus gracilis (nuc-nucleus-gracilis)

clinical.findings: Transection abolishes ipsilateral vibration, joint-position sense and discriminative touch of the lower limb; the gait becomes stamping (sensory ataxia), Romberg sign is positive, and tabes dorsalis or dorsal cord lesions are classic causes.
clinical.note: Deficits are ipsilateral below the lesion because the pathway does not cross until the internal arcuate fibers.

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed., Ch. "Somatosensory Pathways"

name: Nucleus gracilis
function: First synapse of the dorsal column-medial lemniscus pathway for the lower body: primary afferents of the fasciculus gracilis terminate in tonotopically leg-arranged columns, and the second-order neurons emit the internal arcuate fibers that decussate to form the contralateral medial lemniscus. Its dorsal bulge is the gracile tubercle of the closed medulla.

efferent: Internal arcuate fibers (tract-internal-arcuate) to the contralateral medial lemniscus

bloodSupply: Posterior spinal artery; PICA medial branches

clinical.findings: Nuclear or fascicular involvement in medial/dorsal medullary lesions degrades two-point discrimination, vibration and position sense of the contralateral leg after decussation of the second-order axons.

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed., Ch. "Somatosensory Pathways"
Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed., Ch. "Brainstem I: Surface Anatomy and Cross-Sectional Anatomy"

name: Fasciculus cuneatus
function: Lateral dorsal-column bundle conveying uncrossed large-fiber touch, vibration and proprioception from the upper trunk, upper limb and neck (above about T6) to the nucleus cuneatus; present only above midthoracic levels, lying lateral to the fasciculus gracilis throughout the upper cord and closed medulla.

afferent: Upper trunk, upper limb and neck dorsal-root large-fiber afferents
efferent: Nucleus cuneatus (nuc-nucleus-cuneatus)

clinical.syndrome: Ipsilateral upper-limb sensory loss below the decussation
clinical.findings: The cuneate fasciculus carries uncrossed fibres from the arm and hand, so a lesion beneath the sensory decussation — a high cervical fracture-dislocation, a foramen magnum tumour or a Chiari malformation pressing on the dorsal medulla — removes vibration, joint-position sense and discriminative touch from the ipsilateral arm and hand, with pseudoathetosis of the fingers and a positive Romberg sign. Because the cuneate bundle lies lateral to the gracilis, a partial lesion spares the leg.
clinical.note: The bundle exists only above about T6: below that level the upper-limb fibres have not yet entered the cord, so the same lesion cannot produce this pattern.

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed., Ch. "Somatosensory Pathways"

name: Nucleus cuneatus
function: First synapse of the dorsal column-medial lemniscus pathway for the upper body: hand-arm-shoulder-ordered relay of the fasciculus cuneatus whose axons join the internal arcuate decussation; in addition, its rostral accessory (external cuneate) portion relays unconscious upper-limb proprioception to the cerebellum through the inferior cerebellar peduncle. Its dorsal bulge is the cuneate tubercle.

efferent: Internal arcuate fibers (tract-internal-arcuate)
Cuneocerebellar fibers via the inferior cerebellar peduncle (tract-icp)

bloodSupply: Posterior spinal artery; PICA medial branches

clinical.syndrome: Ipsilateral limb ataxia without conscious sensory loss (cuneocerebellar relay)
clinical.findings: The rostral accessory (external cuneate) part of the nucleus relays unconscious upper-limb proprioception to the cerebellum through the inferior cerebellar peduncle, so its involvement in a dorsolateral medullary lesion adds ipsilateral dysmetria and past-pointing of the arm. Destruction of the principal part instead removes conscious vibration and joint-position sense from the ipsilateral arm and hand, because the internal arcuate fibres have not yet crossed.
clinical.vascular: Posterior spinal artery; PICA medial branches
clinical.note: A hyperintense dorsal medullary signal on MRI (subacute combined degeneration of the cord) or an enlarged cuneate tubercle is the imaging correlate of this nucleus failing.

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed., Ch. "Somatosensory Pathways"

name: Principal inferior olivary nucleus
function: The elegantly folded gray lamella that bulges as the olive on the ventrolateral medulla: source of all olivocerebellar climbing fibers, which cross the midline, ascend in the inferior cerebellar peduncle and wrap Purkinje cell dendrites with powerful complex spikes — the teaching (error and timing) signal that drives cerebellar motor learning. Actively regulated by the dentato-rubro-olivary loop via the central tegmental tract.

afferent: Red nucleus via the central tegmental tract (tract-central-tegmental, rubro-olivary fibers)
Nucleo-olivary fibers from the dentate and interposed nuclei
efferent: Olivocerebellar climbing fibers crossing through the inferior cerebellar peduncle (tract-icp) to the contralateral cerebellar cortex

bloodSupply: Direct branches of the vertebral artery; ASA and PICA borderzone

clinical.findings: Transsynaptic degeneration of the olive after a lesion of the Guillain-Mollaret triangle (dentate nucleus, superior cerebellar peduncle, or central tegmental tract), producing palatal (palatopharyngeal) myoclonus/tremor months after the index lesion.
clinical.note: MRI shows T2 hyperintensity with enlargement of the olive (hypertrophic degeneration, not atrophy).

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed., Ch. "Brainstem II: Internal Structures and Vascular Supply"
Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed., Ch. "Cerebellum"

name: Medial accessory olivary nucleus
function: Paramedian subdivision of the olivary complex projecting climbing fibers selectively to the vermis and vestibulocerebellum; a key node of the Guillain-Mollaret triangle, receiving rubro-olivary fibers of the central tegmental tract and giving the medial, most heavily myelinated olivocerebellar stream.

efferent: Climbing fibers to the vermis and vestibulocerebellum via tract-icp

clinical.syndrome: Palatal tremor from hypertrophic olivary degeneration (Guillain-Mollaret triangle)
clinical.findings: When the triangle is interrupted — by a lesion of the central tegmental tract, the dentate nucleus or the superior cerebellar peduncle — the medial accessory olive loses its climbing-fibre target and undergoes trans-synaptic hypertrophy, producing rhythmic 1-3 Hz palatal tremor that persists during sleep, often with synchronous ocular (pendular) and laryngeal movement. The tremor appears weeks to months after the causative stroke.
clinical.note: The olive is disinhibited and hypertrophied rather than destroyed, so MRI shows a swollen, T2-hyperintense inferior olive — the imaging signature of the triangle's interruption.

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed., Ch. "Brainstem II: Internal Structures and Vascular Supply"

name: Medial lemniscus
function: The great ascending band of conscious mechanosensation: formed at the sensory decussation by crossed internal arcuate fibers and ascending alongside the midline to the ventral posterolateral thalamus. In the medulla its fibers are stacked with the leg lateral and the arm medial; the bundle gradually swings laterally and ventrally as it climbs through pons toward its midbrain position.

afferent: Internal arcuate fibers (tract-internal-arcuate) from the gracile and cuneate nuclei
efferent: Ventral posterolateral nucleus (nuc-vpl), thence S1 (tract-dcml composite pathway)

bloodSupply: Anterior spinal artery in the medulla; paramedian basilar perforators in the pons

clinical.findings: Paramedian medullary infarcts (medial medullary syndrome) abolish contralateral vibration, joint-position sense and discriminative touch of the body, with sensory ataxia and positive Romberg; the face is spared because trigeminal modalities travel separately.

clinical.syndrome: Ataxic hemiparesis from a paramedian pontine lacune
clinical.findings: A small lacunar infarct in the paramedian basis pontis or internal capsule can catch the medial lemniscus together with the corticospinal fibres, giving weakness with disproportionate limb ataxia (ataxic hemiparesis, dysarthria-clumsy hand); the mild loss of joint-position sense is easily missed unless vibration and finger-nose testing are performed carefully.
clinical.note: Because the lemniscus hugs the midline throughout the brainstem it is involved in most paramedian brainstem strokes — medullary (Déjerine), pontine and midbrain variants differ only in the accompanying cranial-nerve signs.

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed., Ch. "Somatosensory Pathways"
Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed., Ch. "Brainstem II: Internal Structures and Vascular Supply"

name: Spinal trigeminal tract
function: Dorsolaterally descending bundle of CN V pain-temperature afferents (with contributions from CN VII, IX and X for the ear, pharynx and posterior tongue) running from the principal sensory nucleus to the upper cervical cord alongside the spinal trigeminal nucleus; fibers are somatotopically laminated so that V1 sits most ventral/rostral and V3 most dorsal/caudal — the substrate of the onion-skin pattern.

afferent: Pain-temperature primary afferents of CN V, VII, IX, X from the trigeminal, geniculate and superior-petrosal/inferior ganglia
efferent: Spinal trigeminal nucleus (nuc-spinal-trigeminal)

bloodSupply: PICA and vertebral lateral medullary branches

clinical.findings: Lateral medullary (Wallenberg) infarcts abolish pain and temperature over the ipsilateral face with a characteristic onion-skin gradient, dissociated from facial touch (principal sensory nucleus, rostral pons) and from contralateral body pain loss (spinothalamic tract).

clinical.syndrome: Dissociated facial sensory loss (tract vs principal nucleus)
clinical.findings: The descending tract and its nucleus subserve only pain and temperature, so an incomplete lateral medullary infarct can remove those modalities from the face while light touch and trigeminal motor function stay intact; the same dissociated pattern is produced deliberately by a tractotomy at the obex for intractable facial pain, and the preserved touch is the signature that separates a spinal-tract lesion from a lesion of the principal sensory nucleus in the mid-pons.
clinical.note: Afferents of CN V, VII, IX and X all run here, so lesions can also numb the external ear canal and the posterior tongue and pharynx.

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed., Ch. "Somatosensory Pathways"
Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed., Ch. "Brainstem II: Internal Structures and Vascular Supply"

name: Spinal trigeminal nucleus
function: Long column of second-order facial pain-temperature neurons (subnuclei oralis, interpolaris and caudalis) extending from the caudal pons through the medulla into the upper cervical cord; subnucleus caudalis is the lamina-like pain relay (comparable to the spinal dorsal horn), while rostral parts gate corneal-blink and other trigeminal reflex arcs. Output rises through the ventral trigeminothalamic tract to contralateral VPM.

afferent: Spinal trigeminal tract (tract-spinal-trigeminal) afferents of CN V, VII, IX, X
efferent: Ventral trigeminothalamic tract (tract-trigeminothalamic-ventral)
Reflex interneurons to the facial motor nucleus (blink) and ambiguus (gag)

bloodSupply: PICA / vertebral lateral branches; AICA rostrally

clinical.syndrome: Afferent limb loss of the corneal reflex
clinical.findings: Involvement of the nucleus/tract blunts ipsilateral facial nociception and the blink response to corneal stimulation; combined with ambiguus lesions it also removes the gag afferent-efferent arc components.

clinical.syndrome: Onion-skin facial sensory gradient (subnucleus caudalis topography)
clinical.findings: Subnucleus caudalis is laminated like the dorsal horn, with perioral fibres ending most rostrally, so a lesion of its caudal and dorsal laminae numbs the outer face, ear and scalp while sparing the nose and mouth — the onion-skin pattern of lateral medullary infarction. Because the tract and the nucleus are functionally coupled, a lesion of either is clinically indistinguishable.
clinical.note: The blink (corneal) and gag reflexes are relayed through the rostral subnuclei, which is why a lateral medullary lesion can blunt the corneal reflex as well as pain-temperature sensation.

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed., Ch. "Brainstem II: Internal Structures and Vascular Supply"
Snell, Clinical Neuroanatomy, trigeminal system sections

name: Nucleus solitarius (cardiorespiratory part)
function: The visceral afferent hub of the dorsomedial medulla: first synapse for CN IX and CN X general visceral afferents — carotid-body chemoreceptors and carotid-sinus baroreceptors, aortic arch receptors, pulmonary stretch fibers, laryngeal-pharyngeal sensation and gastrointestinal afferents. Its neurons compute the reflexes controlling blood pressure, respiration, swallowing and GI motility, and project to the dorsal motor vagal nucleus, nucleus ambiguus and the ventrolateral medullary vasomotor/respiratory columns.

afferent: CN IX carotid body/sinus and pharyngeal afferents
CN X aortic, pulmonary, laryngeal and gastrointestinal afferents
efferent: Dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus (nuc-dmv)
Nucleus ambiguus (nuc-ambiguus) for swallow/gag motor arc
Ventrolateral medulla (respiratory and vasomotor columns)
Hypothalamus and parabrachial nuclei (visceral-limbic relay)

clinical.findings: Bilateral NTS or its afferent-nerve damage abolishes baroreceptor buffering, yielding volatile hypertension-tachycardia crises alternating with hypotension; unilateral lateral medullary infarcts acutely raise blood pressure and impair chemoreceptor (hypoxic) drive.
Loss of pharyngolaryngeal afferent processing contributes to post-stroke dysphagia and aspiration in lateral medullary strokes, together with ambiguus efferent failure.

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed., Ch. "Brainstem II: Internal Structures and Vascular Supply"
Fix, High-Yield Neuroanatomy, autonomic nervous system section

name: Dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus (CN X)
function: Preganglionic parasympathetic column lying under the vagal trigone of the fourth-ventricle floor: its fibers ride the vagus to terminal ganglia of the heart (slowing rate), airways and the enteric wall, driving visceral smooth-muscle motility, secretion and vagal cardiovascular reflexes; baroreceptor information reaches it from the solitary nucleus.

efferent: Vagal preganglionic parasympathetic fibers to cardiac, pulmonary and enteric ganglia

clinical.syndrome: Vagal dysregulation after lateral medullary stroke
clinical.findings: Involvement contributes to dysphagia, gastric stasis, bradyarrhythmias and impaired vagal reflexes in Wallenberg infarcts; bilateral dorsal medullary damage threatens vagal control of viscera.

Vagal preganglionic neurons here slow the heart, drive bronchial secretion and run the enteric motor programme, so dorsal medullary lesions — syringobulbia, Chiari malformation, posterior-fossa surgery, or paramedian extension of a lateral medullary infarct — remove beat-to-beat cardiac modulation, producing bradycardia or asystole, delayed gastric emptying and vomiting; bilateral involvement is needed for the full picture.
clinical.note: Cough syncope and swallowing-induced bradycardia appearing after posterior-fossa surgery are the practical warning signs of dorsal vagal nuclear injury.

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed., Ch. "Brainstem II: Internal Structures and Vascular Supply"

name: Nucleus ambiguus
function: Branchiomotor column deep in the reticular formation sending LMNs through CN IX, CN X and the cranial root of CN XI to the striated muscles of the soft palate, pharynx and larynx — palatal elevation, pharyngeal constriction, vocal-fold abduction for airway protection and phonation. Solitarius afferents complete the swallow and gag reflex arcs through it.

efferent: CN IX to stylopharyngeus
CN X to palate-pharynx-larynx muscles
Cranial XI rootlets to laryngeal adductors

clinical.findings: Unilateral ambiguityus failure droops the ipsilateral palate, paralyzes the ipsilateral vocal fold and destroys effective swallowing — the clinical core of the lateral medullary (Wallenberg) syndrome; aspiration pneumonia is the principal risk.

clinical.syndrome: Progressive bulbar palsy (bulbar-onset motor neuron disease)
clinical.findings: Selective degeneration of the branchiomotor neurons of the nucleus ambiguus — together with the hypoglossal and facial nuclei — produces progressive flaccid dysarthria, nasal regurgitation, choking on liquids and tongue wasting with fasciculations, whereas the pseudobulbar variant instead gives spastic dysarthria with emotional lability. Swallowing failure and aspiration are the leading causes of death in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis.
clinical.note: The nucleus sits deep in the lateral tegmentum, so bilateral involvement — motor neuron disease, a brainstem glioma or vascular disease on both sides — is needed for complete laryngeal paralysis.

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed., Ch. "Brainstem II: Internal Structures and Vascular Supply"
Midbrain, Pons, and Medulla: Anatomy and Syndromes, RadioGraphics 2019 (doi 10.1148/rg.2019180126)

name: Hypoglossal nucleus (CN XII)
function: Paramedian column of LMNs under the hypoglossal trigone of the ventricular floor innervating all intrinsic and extrinsic tongue muscles except the palatoglossus; its bulge helps shape the floor of the fourth ventricle. Corticobulbar input to hypoglossal motoneurons (notably genioglossus) is predominantly contralateral.

afferent: Solitary and reticular viscerosensory inputs (taste-driven feeding reflexes)
efferent: CN XII rootlets through the preolivary sulcus (surf-cn12-exit) to tongue musculature

bloodSupply: Anterior spinal artery (paramedian branches of the vertebral artery)

clinical.findings: Nuclear or rootlet destruction wastes the ipsilateral tongue, which fasciculates and deviates TOWARD the lesion on protrusion (the intact contralateral genioglossus pushes the tip across) — a feature of medial medullary syndrome.
clinical.note: UMN lesions deviate the tongue away from the cerebral lesion (toward the weak side) without wasting or fasciculations.

clinical.syndrome: Bilateral hypoglossal palsy — immobile, wasted tongue
clinical.findings: Bilateral nuclear or rootlet lesions — motor neuron disease, syringobulbia, a midline medullary lesion or bilateral medial medullary infarcts — leave a tongue that can neither be protruded nor moved side to side, with severe dysarthria, pooling of saliva and inability to propel a food bolus; wasting and fasciculations separate it from the spastic, non-wasted tongue of pseudobulbar palsy.
clinical.note: The nucleus bulges into the fourth-ventricle floor as the hypoglossal trigone, the surface landmark used to find it on the medullary plate.

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed., Ch. "Brainstem II: Internal Structures and Vascular Supply"
Patten, Neurological Differential Diagnosis, 2nd ed., cranial nerve examination sections

name: Area postrema
function: Paired circumventricular organ flanking the obex at the caudal floor of the fourth ventricle; because it lacks a blood-brain barrier, it samples blood-borne toxins, drugs and circulating cytokines and triggers the vomiting reflex through the adjacent solitary nucleus and medullary reticular-vagal emetic circuitry — the neural chemoreceptor trigger zone.

afferent: Blood-borne and CSF-borne chemical signals (no blood-brain barrier)
Vagal afferents via the solitary nucleus
efferent: Nucleus solitarius (nuc-solitarius-caudal)
Medullary reticular emetic pattern generators and dorsal vagal complex

clinical.findings: Irritation or infarction of the area postrema (PICA territory) produces severe vertigo with violent vomiting and hiccups, often mimicking vestibular neuritis or gastritis and delaying stroke diagnosis.

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed., Ch. "Brainstem II: Internal Structures and Vascular Supply"
Fix, High-Yield Neuroanatomy, circumventricular organs table

name: Inferior cerebellar peduncle
function: The dominant afferent gateway of the cerebellum: the dorsolateral column formed in the upper medulla by olivocerebellar climbing fibers, cuneocerebellar and posterior spinocerebellar fibers, vestibulocerebellar fibers and reticulocerebellar fibers, all entering the vermis and hemispheres; the juxtarestiform body carries the vestibular portion.

efferent: Cerebellar vermis and hemisphere cortex (ctx-cerebellum)

clinical.findings: Lateral medullary infarcts involving the restiform body yield ipsilateral dysmetria, intention tremor and past-pointing together with vertigo from the adjoining vestibular nuclei.

clinical.syndrome: Partial lateral medullary syndrome — isolated vertigo and ataxia
clinical.findings: A small PICA or vertebral branch infarct confined to the dorsolateral medulla can involve the restiform body and the adjacent vestibular nuclei alone, so the patient presents with acute vertigo, nausea, nystagmus and ipsilateral limb-trunk ataxia that mimics vestibular neuritis. The discriminators are the ipsilateral dysmetria and past-pointing plus lateropulsion, which a peripheral lesion does not produce; HINTS bedside testing (normal head impulse, direction-changing nystagmus, skew deviation) identifies the central cause.
clinical.note: This 'vestibular pseudo-neuritis' presentation is one of the commonest reasons a posterior-circulation stroke is missed in the emergency department.

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed., Ch. "Brainstem II: Internal Structures and Vascular Supply"
Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed., Ch. "Cerebellum"

name: Arcuate nucleus (medulla)
function: Superficial paramedian cell groups astride the pyramids, homologous to the pontine nuclei: they receive descending cortical fibers and relay to the cerebellum through ventral external arcuate fibers that cross and join the inferior cerebellar peduncle; also described as a chemosensitive (CO2/pH) region of the ventral medullary surface.

efferent: Ventral external arcuate fibers to the contralateral cerebellum via tract-icp

clinical.syndrome: Central hypoventilation from ventral medullary chemoreceptor damage
clinical.findings: The superficial arcuate (chemo-sensitive) region on the ventral medullary surface detects CO2 and pH, so damage over it — surgery for a foramen magnum or vertebral lesion, subarachnoid haemorrhage, or a ventral medullary infarct — flattens the CO2 ventilatory response: the patient hypoventilates and sleeps apnoeically with a normal chest examination. Congenital loss of these neurons underlies central congenital hypoventilation (Ondine's curse).
clinical.note: The arcuate nucleus is the medullary homologue of the pontine nuclei: its crossed ventral external arcuate fibres carry cortical copies of movement to the cerebellum through the inferior cerebellar peduncle.

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed., Ch. "Brainstem I: Surface Anatomy and Cross-Sectional Anatomy"

name: Medullary reticular formation
synonyms: central/medial reticular nuclei of the medulla
function: Gigantocellular and central-medial reticular nuclei filling the intermediate tegmentum: source of the medullary (lateral) reticulospinal tract that inhibits antigravity tone and refines posture, site of ventrolateral respiratory column and vasomotor (pressure) integration with the solitary nucleus, and upward continuation of the reticular activating system; premotor autonomic fibers descend to the spinal intermediolateral column.

efferent: Medullary reticulospinal tract (tract-reticulospinal)
Ascending arousal projections to the intralaminar thalamic nuclei
Premotor autonomic fibers to spinal sympathetic neurons

bloodSupply: Vertebral and PICA branches; ASA paramedian branches

clinical.findings: Bilateral damage of the ventrolateral medullary respiratory columns (syringobulbia, lateral medullary extension, high cervical-medullary surgery) removes automatic breathing — patients breathe only when awake (Ondine curse), with apnea and hypercapnia during sleep.
Lateral medullary strokes that irritate the rostral ventrolateral pressor area acutely elevate blood pressure and mimic hypertensive emergencies at presentation.
Involvement of the descending hypothalamospinal sympathetic fibers coursing through the lateral reticular tegmentum yields ipsilateral ptosis and miosis as part of Wallenberg syndrome.

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed., Ch. "Brainstem II: Internal Structures and Vascular Supply"
Fix, High-Yield Neuroanatomy, reticular formation and respiration sections

name: Fourth ventricle
function: Tent-shaped midline CSF cavity between the dorsal pons and medulla in front and the cerebellum behind, continuous rostrally with the cerebral aqueduct and caudally with the central canal at the obex; CSF leaves it through the lateral foramina of Luschka and the midline foramen of Magendie into the subarachnoid space. Its floor carries the facial colliculus, hypoglossal trigone and vagal trigone.

clinical.findings: Tumors of the floor or roof (ependymoma, medulloblastoma) or outflow blockage of Luschka/Magendie trap CSF and raise intracranial pressure with headache, vomiting and papilledema.
clinical.note: The choroid plexus of the roof (tela choroidea) is a principal CSF production site of the posterior fossa.

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed., Ch. "Brainstem I: Surface Anatomy and Cross-Sectional Anatomy"
Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed., Ch. "Brain and Environs" (ventricular system)

name: Glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) exit
function: Rootlets of CN IX emerging from the postolivary sulcus just rostral to the vagal rows: motor fibers to stylopharyngeus (from the nucleus ambiguus), parasympathetic fibers to the parotid (inferior salivatory) and afferents for oropharyngeal sensation, tonsil-posterior tongue taste and carotid sinus-body baroreceptor-chemoreceptor information — the afferent limb of the gag reflex.

clinical.findings: Lateral medullary lesions or root-zone damage abolish ipsilateral pharyngeal sensation and the gag response, with loss of the carotid sinus reflex (swinging blood pressure).

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed., Ch. "Brainstem I: Surface Anatomy and Cross-Sectional Anatomy"

name: Vagus nerve (CN X) exit
function: Rows of vagal rootlets leaving the postolivary sulcus below CN IX, carrying fibers from the dorsal motor nucleus (parasympathetic viscera), nucleus ambiguus (palate-pharynx-larynx striated muscle) and returning visceral afferents from thoracic and abdominal viscera through the solitary complex.

clinical.findings: Combined with ambiguus damage, produces hoarseness, depressed gag/efferent response, dysphagia and loss of cough reflex sensation on the ipsilateral side.

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed., Ch. "Brainstem I: Surface Anatomy and Cross-Sectional Anatomy"

name: Accessory nerve (CN XI) exit
synonyms: cranial and spinal roots of CN XI
function: Cranial rootlets from the caudal ambiguus leave the postolivary sulcus and are joined by spinal rootlets ascending through the foramen magnum from C1-C5; the combined nerve exits the jugular foramen to innervate sternocleidomastoid and trapezius (with the cranial portion hitching onto the vagus for laryngeal adduction).

clinical.findings: Unilateral CN XI damage wastes ipsilateral sternocleidomastoid (weak contralateral head rotation) and trapezius (shoulder droop, scapular winging); foramen magnum and jugular foramen lesions are the classic localizers.
clinical.note: The spinal rootlets climbing the lateral medulla are tagged on the closed-medulla plates.

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed., Ch. "Brainstem I: Surface Anatomy and Cross-Sectional Anatomy"

name: Hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) exit
function: Rootlets of CN XII emerging between pyramid and olive at the preolivary sulcus and collecting into the hypoglossal nerve through the hypoglossal canal; these are the axons of the hypoglossal nucleus en route to all tongue muscles except palatoglossus.

clinical.findings: Medial medullary infarcts involving the exiting rootlets deviate the protruded tongue toward the lesion with eventual ipsilateral wasting — paired with contralateral hemiparesis and lemniscal sensory loss.

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed., Ch. "Brainstem I: Surface Anatomy and Cross-Sectional Anatomy"

name: Obex
synonyms: caudal apex of the fourth ventricle
function: The caudal apex of the fourth ventricle where its roof narrows into the central canal; flanked by the area postrema and gracile tubercles, it marks the cervicomedullary transition on the dorsal surface and is the key surgical and radiologic landmark of the posterior fossa outlet.

clinical.findings: Tonsillar herniation (Chiari I) is measured against the obex-foramen magnum line; lesions around the obex (syringobulbia, tumors) affect the area postrema and NTS with emesis and autonomic instability.
clinical.note: Open-medulla plates key the ventricle apex to the obex (lvl-olivary).

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed., Ch. "Brainstem I: Surface Anatomy and Cross-Sectional Anatomy"

name: Cerebellar hemispheres and vermis (context)
function: Envelope of the cerebellum — two lateral hemispheres joined by the midline vermis dorsal to the pons and medulla. The lateral (neocerebellar) hemispheres plan skilled limb movements through the dentato-thalamo-cortical loop, the intermediate zone corrects ongoing limb trajectories via the interposed nuclei, and the vermis and flocculonodular lobe govern axial posture, gait and balance-eye coordination. Cerebellar output acts ipsilateral to the body because its efferents cross twice.

afferent: Middle cerebellar peduncle (tract-mcp) — crossed pontocerebellar fibers
Inferior cerebellar peduncle (tract-icp) — climbing, spinocerebellar and vestibulocerebellar fibers
efferent: Superior cerebellar peduncle (tract-scp) — dentate/interposed/fastigial output to contralateral thalamus, red nucleus and reticular formation

bloodSupply: Superior cerebellar artery (SCA) superiorly, anterior inferior cerebellar artery (AICA) anteriorly, posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA) inferiorly

clinical.findings: Hemisphere lesions produce ipsilateral dysmetria, intention (terminal) tremor, dysdiadochokinesia, hypotonia and rebound; gait is broad-based and veers toward the lesion.
Midline (vermal) involvement produces falling and staggering with relatively preserved limb coordination on the bed — typical of midline tumors and alcohol-related vermal atrophy.

contextNote: Context envelope for the 3D scene and sagittal/coronal plates (two hemispheres plus vermis bar); the deep nuclei and vermis are separate records, and the peduncles are owned elsewhere: tract-mcp (pons), tract-icp (medulla), tract-scp (midbrain).
refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed., Ch. "Cerebellum"
Nolte, The Human Brain, cerebellum chapter

name: Dentate nucleus
function: The largest deep cerebellar nucleus, a convoluted gray ribbon in the lateral (neocerebellar) white matter: it collects inhibitory Purkinje output from the lateral hemispheres and fires the dentato-thalamo-cortical loop through the superior cerebellar peduncle to the contralateral VL/VA thalamus and red nucleus — the efferent side of motor planning, movement timing and cognitive-linguistic sequencing.

afferent: Purkinje cell axons of the lateral cerebellar hemispheres
Collaterals of the tract-mcp (pontocerebellar) and tract-scp systems
efferent: Superior cerebellar peduncle (tract-scp) decussating to contralateral VL/VA thalamus and red nucleus

clinical.findings: SCA infarcts or lesions of the dentate/SCP system produce ipsilateral intention tremor, dysmetria and decomposition of movement; bilateral dentate disease (Ceroid-lipofuscinosis, metronomic injury) disturbs movement timing.
Dentate or SCP lesions interrupt the dentato-rubro-olivary triangle and secondarily degenerate the inferior olive, causing palatal myoclonus.
clinical.note: Links the dentate to the medullary olive via the contralateral red nucleus.

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed., Ch. "Cerebellum"
Fix, High-Yield Neuroanatomy, deep cerebellar nuclei table

name: Interposed nuclei (emboliform and globose)
function: Combined emboliform and globose nuclei of the intermediate (paravermal) spinocerebellum: they gate Purkinje output that compares intended with ongoing limb movement and fire the correction loop through the superior cerebellar peduncle to the magnocellular red nucleus (rubrospinal) and VL thalamus — the on-line limb stabilizer.

afferent: Purkinje axons of the paravermal intermediate zone
efferent: Superior cerebellar peduncle (tract-scp) to the red nucleus and VL thalamus

clinical.syndrome: Ipsilateral limb dysmetria from interposed-nucleus loss
clinical.findings: The interposed (emboliform and globose) nuclei are the output of the intermediate spinocerebellum, so their destruction removes the on-line correction of ongoing limb movement: the ipsilateral arm overshoots and oscillates on finger-to-nose testing, with dysdiadochokinesia, hypotonia and a coarse intention tremor, while trunk control and gait are comparatively spared because the vermis and fastigial loop are intact.
clinical.note: Signs are ipsilateral because cerebellar outflow crosses twice (SCP decussation, then the cortical projection); the interposed output reaches the magnocellular red nucleus through the superior cerebellar peduncle.

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed., Ch. "Cerebellum"

name: Fastigial nucleus
function: Medialmost deep nucleus of the vermis and vestibulocerebellum: receives vermal Purkinje output and drives axial posture and eye-position control through fibers that leave via the inferior cerebellar peduncle to vestibular and reticular nuclei and via the superior cerebellar peduncle to the contralateral VL and central tegmental tract — calibration of balance, gait and the vestibulo-ocular reflex.

afferent: Purkinje axons of the vermis (ctx-cerebellum midline) and flocculonodular lobe
efferent: Vestibular and reticular nuclei via tract-icp
Contralateral VL thalamus and red nucleus region via tract-scp

clinical.findings: Fastigial or vermal lesions give a wide-based staggering gait with truncal instability and nystagmus while limb coordination on the bed may be preserved; bilateral posterior fossa lesions therefore present predominantly as gait ataxia.

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed., Ch. "Cerebellum"

name: Vermis
function: The midline cerebellar strip separating the hemispheres on the dorsal surface, containing the vermal (axial body) representation of the spinocerebellum and, caudally, the uvula-nodulus of the vestibulocerebellum; governs trunk and proximal gait musculature and, with the nodulus-flocculus, gaze-holding and balance.

clinical.findings: Midline vermal damage — midline posterior fossa tumors (medulloblastoma), alcohol atrophy of the anterior vermis — causes staggering, wide-based gait with falls and impaired tandem walking, with little limb dysmetria; children with vermal tumors present with gait ataxia plus morning vomiting.

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed., Ch. "Cerebellum"

name: Medulla (context surface)
function: Renderable silhouette of the medulla oblongata as one block: the ventral pyramids with their decussation, the olives produced by the inferior olivary complex, the dorsal column gracile and cuneate tubercles, the postolivary and preolivary sulci carrying the CN IX-XII rootlets, and the floor of the open fourth ventricle caudally. It exists so the medulla is a single named, selectable body in the 3D scene and on the plate outlines, not because it is a nucleus; the internal content belongs to its own records.
